newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole arrive for debate; pressure on Dole.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole arrive for debate; pressure on Dole.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole arrived in Connecticut on Sunday for the first presidential debate with all the pressure on Dole to diminish an aura of inevitability beginning to surround Clinton's re-election bid.
After months of shadow boxing, the candidates were to meet for 90 minutes in Hartford's Bushnell Theatre to answer questions posed by moderator Jim Lehrer of the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS).

Clinton was first to arrive on a beautiful, clear, chilly day. He drove straight from the airport to check the sound and lighting at the debate site, after playing cards with aides on the brief plane ride from Buffalo, New York.
"He wanted to do one thing today he could win for sure," said White House press secretary Mike McCurry.

Later, the president addressed several hundred supporters who gathered outside his hotel. "Tonight, I'm going to have a chance to tell the American people what you know already -- we are better off than we were four years ago," he said.

Dole landed 90 minutes after Clinton and headed for his own tour of the site. He then checked into a suburban hotel to rest for the encounter and was greeted by hundreds of cheering people carrying "Dole/Kemp" placards. He and his wife Elizabeth gave the crowd "thumbs up" signs before seeking a few hours of quiet.

Connecticut's Republican Gov. John Rowland said Dole's task was to "unmask Bill Clinton" while projecting his own message to an audience that may approach 90 million people. At the same time, Dole had to stay positive and keep the harsher side of his personality in check.
"The debate is much more important for Bob Dole than for Bill Clinton. Bill Clinton is just sitting on his lead, running out the clock," Rowland said.

A Reuters/Zogby daily tracking poll on Sunday found Clinton still more than 15 percentage points ahead of Dole. "Bill Clinton is in amazingly good shape going into the debate," pollster John Zogby said.

Still, Dole campaign officials insisted Clinton's support was soft and could crumble after strong showings by the Republican nominee in this and the second presidential debate on Oct. 16 in San Diego.
"Bob Dole gets the first chance to speak without a filter to share the vision that he has," Dole's running mate Jack Kemp said on NBC Television's "Meet the Press" programme.
Clinton, in an interview with the Hartford Courant newspaper, said he would try to avoid scoring cheap debating points and concentrate on the big issues facing the country.

"The thing that I want to do is to keep my mind focused on what I say to people out there in the audience, how this thing relates to the American people and their future and not just score points," Clinton said.

The president is generally seen as the better communicator so expectations may be higher for him than for Dole. Muddying the waters were rumours emanating from the Dole camp that the Republican nominee might be preparing a surprise, possibly in the form of a "mystery guest" sitting in the front row of the audience, to unnerve Clinton.

Dole brought one guest with him on his plane -- 75-year-old New Yorker Frank Carafa, a son of Italian immigrants who saved Dole's life by pulling him to safety from a World War Two battlefield in Italy where Dole had been badly shot and left for dead.
During the flight to Hartford, Carafa told a moving story of how he saved Dole by braving a hail of German bullets to pull him from a ravine to safety.

There were some reports Dole might even use the debate as an opportunity to state his intention of naming popular retired Gen. Colin Powell as his secretary of state if he won the election. Dole has repeatedly said he might name prospective cabinet members before Election Day.

One issue likely to come up in the debates was whether Clinton would rule out issuing pardons to some of his friends and associates convicted in cases connected to the Whitewater affair, a complex web of land and tax deals that has dogged the president and his wife for the past four years.

The Reuters poll found that 40 percent of respondents would be less likely to vote for Clinton if he issued pardons. But 43 percent said it would make no difference to their vote and 19 percent would be more likely to vote for Clinton.
